idiom_name: lambda expressions capturing the former locals by reference
implementation_notes: Modern default: since C++11 a lambda expression is an unnamed closure object that captures the enclosing function's variables, so the decomposed steps become lambdas declared after their locals and capturing them by reference ([&]); no class has to be written and, for a stack-local lambda, no allocation is required. A lambda body cannot itself be split into member functions, so when the algorithm needs several named steps sharing one object, either declare several lambdas over the same locals (they share the underlying variables) or take the local-functor variant. Keep [&] lambdas strictly non-escaping: a closure that outlives the enclosing function leaves dangling references.
pitfalls: A lambda capturing by reference must not escape the enclosing function; storing it in a std::function or returning it leaves dangling references.
By-copy captures are const inside the closure unless the lambda is declared mutable, and each by-copy capture of a large object copies it when the closure is created.
Several [&] lambdas that mutate the same local share it, which is convenient here but makes the data flow invisible; a named local struct is clearer once the set grows.

variants.name: Local functor with operator() (C++98 class form)
variants.idiom_name: class holding the former locals with the algorithm split into member functions
variants.implementation_notes: The faithful C++ form and the only one available before C++11: define a class - at namespace scope, or locally inside the function when it is used nowhere else - with data members for the receiver, the arguments and the former locals, plus member functions for the steps and an operator() (or call()) entry point that runs them in order. Choose it over lambdas when the steps need names, the algorithm wants to be unit-tested directly, or the closure would capture a large environment; a namespace-scope class also compiles on pre-C++11 toolchains.
pitfalls: A local class could not be used to instantiate templates before C++11, so a local functor passed to std::function or a template algorithm will not compile on older standards.
Members initialise in declaration order, so a functor whose constructor derives one field from another must not depend on constructor argument order.
Reusing one functor instance for several computations is the same defect as caching a method object; construct a fresh one per invocation.
